plan.description: Seagrass ecosystems are considered key blue carbon sinks due to their capacity to store particulate organic carbon in the sediments. However, other mechanisms of carbon sequestration remain understudied, such as outwelling or export of recalcitrant dissolved carbon. This project aims to unravel these pathways through the study of how theseecosystems influence the seawater carbonate system in present and future climatic conditions. Using advanced instrumentation at Kristineberg Centre—Picarro gas analysers, automatic alkalinity titrators, spectrophotometers, and nutrient analysis facilities— together with in situ field measurements in nearby meadows; the study will assess fluxes of multiple carbon species and greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O). Results will determine whether these ecosystems act as carbon sinks or sources. Expected outcomes include improved understanding of the role of seagrasses in coastal carbon budgets and guidance for their inclusion in climate mitigation strategies.

description.description: In this project, no work involves human participants, personal data, human cells or tissues, animals, non‑EU countries, artificial intelligence, or any activity that could generate dual‑use concerns. The only ethical dimension relates to the project’s interaction with the natural environment, specifically the temporary installation of non‑destructive sensors and benthic chambers in seagrass meadows and the collection of a small number of seagrass shoots for biomass measurements. The project follows the “Do No Harm” principle, applying strict safeguards to avoid ecological disturbance in protected habitats. All deployments use established, non‑invasive techniques that have repeatedly shown no detectable impact on seagrass structure, sediment stability, or ecosystem functioning. Biomass sampling is minimal, spatially distributed, and far below thresholds known to affect meadow integrity. The project is adherent to responsible research practices, including environmental stewardship, transparency, open science, and compliance with institutional safety procedures. No intellectual property is expected to arise from the work, and all research outputs will be openly shared.

fieldSet.title: Data Publication Repository
fieldSet.description:
In which repository, database, or data catalogue will you publish your data set(s)? Please indicate a publication venue for each of your data types or data sets, if you will publish in more than one place. 

Recommedations:

If you are doing organismal experimentation, use the following services/repositories:

  • BioStudies - for study metadata and result data in tabular format, with some scope to include images (depending on size). All organismal studies should include a BioStudies accession to record project metadata, and possibly to deposit result data
  •  BioSamples - to register organismal samples in the BioStudies accession and add sample specific metadata 
  •  EMBL ENA - for sequence data, incl. metagenomics, transciptomics, etc
  • ArrayExpress - microarray or qPCR data
  • ChEMBL - molecular assay results, structures, etc…
  • Metabolights - for spectrographic data (LC-MS, UV-vis, etc)
  • Protocols.IO - for protocols if these are an output
  • EurOBIS - for biodiversity data
  • Ecotaxa - for biodiversity imaging
  • BioImage Archive - for other types of biological image
  • Seanoe -  for other types of marine-derived data (not better placed above)
  • Pangaea - everything else Earth Science related, but not marine (very broad)
If you are collecting only environmental/physical data (that is not organismal sample metadata), consider using:
  • SeaDataNet
  • Seanoe
Only if there is not a more data-specific repository you could use should you use Zenodo or Figshare, or some other (unstructured) repository - this is likely to be a very rare occurance. If in doubt, please contact the AQUASERV Helpdesk

You may be required to archive your data in a repository of your university/organisation. If that repository is not accessible to everyone, then you should also publish your data in one of these other mentioned repositories. But even if that is open to everyone, you should publish in one of these other mentioned repositories as your data are more globally findable in those.

fieldSet.title: Metadata collection
fieldSet.description:
How will you collect your dataset description and provenance metadata? 

Reminder: metadata are the descriptive data that contextualise and describe the actual data themselves and make your data findable, re-usable, and reproducible. This includes information that describe these aspects:
  • WHO - did the work
  • WHEN - was the work done
  • WHERE - was the work conducted, the field work/sampling done
  • WHAT - parameters and samples (use BioSamples accessions if appropriate) did you collect/work with
  • WHAT - instruments, software, platforms wer used
  • WHAT - what data files are in your data set and what do they contain 
  • HOW - were the sampling, sample processing, experiments, and software analysis done (register methods and protocols with protocols.io)
If you create a BioStudies accession for your project, then your data can be included in that accession and linked to any other data you publish in other repositories.

Examples
WHO, WHEN, and WHERE
I will collect the following information in a spreadsheet: the names and ORCID IDs of all the people involved in the work, the coordinates of my sampling field work, the name of service provider where I did the work, the dates of the sample collection and the subsequent sample and data processing.
I will include these information in the metadata form when I publish my data on BioStudies. 

WHAT
I will ask the TA service provider for the types/names and IDs of all the instruments and devices I will use.
My samples will be given an ID that I will create, and these IDs will be included in my experimental data and be linked to all photographs I take of the specimens. 
My samples will also be documented with the WoRMS species names. 
I will record the name and version of the software that I used (it will be my own software that I will subsequentely make available via GitHub).
I will create a README to describe each file in my data set. 
I will include these information in the metadata form when I publish my data on BioStudies.

HOW
I will also ask the TA service provider for the URL/DOI of their protocols that I followed and will record this in my README. If those protocols are not published, I will instead ask for a PDF copy and I will include this as part of my dataset. 
I will publish my own protocol on the protocols.io AQUASERV Community. I will then add all the DOI to my README.
I will only use my own software, and the settings will be included within the code I will publish. 
I will include these information in the metadata form when I publish my data on BioStudies.

fieldSet.title: Open Data Formats
fieldSet.description:
Are the formats in which you publish your data open?

If NO: please list the non-open formats and explain why you have to use them.

A closed format needs a proprietary software application to be read (i.e. typical examples are spreadsheets in MS Excel format xlsx. Some instruments (e.g. LC-MS) also produce data that can only be read by proprietary (commercial) instrument-specific software - these data should be converted to open formats before publication. 
An open format can be opened and read by anyone without needing specific software to do that. Examples are: CSV, TSV, FASTA, FASTQ, PDF, JPG
If in doubt: try wikipedia! 

NB some formats are not open but are openable with free software: for example, MP4 and XLSX. If you can convert these to open formats (e.g. CSV instead of XLSX), please do so.  

Examples
  • The instruments I will use at the TA station produce data in proprietary formats: I will discuss with the TA station how I can convert these to open formats before publication.
  • I will convert my MS Excel files to CSV before I publish them, so they are in an open format

fieldSet.title: Vocabularies and Ontologies
fieldSet.description:
Will you use controlled vocabularies or ontologies in your data and metadata?

Controlled vocabularies contain terms that are agreed by scientific communities working within the field of expertise. These terms are written in a controlled way and have one definition that everyone has agreed on. The terms can be found on the web via a URL (web address), and will have an ID by which they can be referred to as well as the actual term name (a string). 
Ontologies are glorified vocabularies, as they additionally ascribe meaning and relations between terms of a vocabulary. 

Examples are:
  • MIXS - Minimum Information about any (x) Sequence (MIxS) standard
  • ENVO - The Environment Ontology
  • Marine Regions - A standard list of marine georeferenced place names
  • EDAM - Ontology of bioscientific data analysis and data management
  • EFO - Experimental Factor Ontology
  • WoRMS -  World Register of Marine Species
  • NCBI Taxonomy Database - Classification and nomenclature for all organisms

Examples
  • I will use terms from ENVO to describe the habitats relevant to my experiment. I will use their recommended URLs for the terms   (http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/ENVO_12345678)
  • I will use NVS to describe measured parameters and their units. I will use their recommended URLs for the terms  (http://vocab.nerc.ac.uk/collection/P01/current/ABCDEDG/)
  • I will use MiXS when uploading my data to ENA, as this is mandatory
  • I will use NCBI taxonomy for all taxon names, and will use their recommended IDs for the names (NCBI:txid123456)

field.textValue:
Yes, but only in a limited and contextual way.

1. Climate projection data
The project will re‑use IPCC climate projections (RCP 8.5) to define the “future conditions” treatment in the benthic chamber experiments (increased temperature and CO₂). Source: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), publicly available reports and datasets. Purpose: To set realistic end‑of‑century warming and acidification scenarios for experimental manipulation.

2. Environmental baselines (if needed)
If required for comparison or calibration, the project may consult existing environmental baseline data from the Kristineberg Marine Research Station (e.g., long‑term temperature, salinity, or pH records). Source: Kristineberg Centre / University of Gothenburg monitoring programmes. Purpose: To contextualise short‑term field measurements within long‑term environmental variability.
I will archive the data in a repository from the institution where I work (CSIC).

1. Parameter and Unit Vocabularies (NVS / SeaDataNet / BODC)
I will use the NERC Vocabulary Server (NVS) collections, especially:
  • P01 – BODC Parameter Usage Vocabulary (e.g., DIC, TA, CH₄, N₂O, nutrients)
  • P06 – Units vocabulary
  • L22 – Instrument vocabulary (e.g., Picarro GHG analyser, multiparameter sensors)
These vocabularies are standard in marine biogeochemistry and are required by most repositories.

2. Environmental and Habitat Ontologies (ENVO)
I will use ENVO (Environment Ontology) terms to describe:
  • Seagrass meadows
  • Coastal marine habitats
  • Sediment types
  • Water column descriptors
3. Marine Regions Gazetteer
I will use Marine Regions for:
  • Standardised geographic names
  • Region identifiers for Gullmar Fjord and sampling sites
4. SeaDataNet / CF Standard Names
For environmental variables and sensor time series, I will use:
  • CF Standard Names (e.g., temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen)
  • SeaDataNet vocabularies for oceanographic parameters
6. Species Names
Although the project does not focus on taxonomic sampling, any reference to seagrass species will use:
  • WoRMS – World Register of Marine Species: Zostera marina (AphiaID: 145784)
To give time to publish the sicence. As soon as it is pubished, all data will be published as well.

1. WHO – People involved
I will record, with a metadata spreadsheet (CSV):
  • Full names and ORCID IDs of all contributors
  • Roles (field sampling, laboratory analysis, data processing, supervision)
  • Affiliation (Kristineberg Marine Research Station, ICM‑CSIC, etc.)
2. WHEN – Dates of all activities
I will document, with field logs, laboratory logs, and metadata spreadsheets:
  • Dates of fieldwork (deployment, sampling, retrieval)
  • Dates of laboratory analyses (GHG, TA, pH, nutrients, PIC/POC/DIC)
  • Dates of data processing and modelling
3. WHERE – Location of sampling and work
I will record with Field notebooks, GPS exports, and metadata:
  • GPS coordinates of each benthic chamber deployment
  • Site names within the Gullmar Fjord
  • Laboratory locations (Kristineberg Centre, SWEDAC‑accredited labs)
4. WHAT – Samples, parameters, instruments, and files
I will document with metadata spreadsheets, README files, and repository metadata forms:

Samples and parameters
  • Sample IDs for all water, sediment, and biomass samples
  • Treatment (vegetated vs non‑vegetated; present vs future conditions)
  • Parameters measured (DIC, TA, pH, CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, nutrients, PIC/POC/DIC, chlorophyll)

Instruments and platforms
  • Instrument names, models, and serial numbers: Picarro GHG analyser, Spectrophotometer, Automatic alkalinity titrator, Multiparameter sensors
  • Calibration information when available
  • Software used (R version, seacarb version, etc.)
Data files
  • A README describing each file, its structure, units, and variables
  • A data dictionary defining all variables and units
  • A workflow description linking raw data → processed data → outputs
5. HOW – Methods, protocols, and workflows
I will document:
  • Field protocols for benthic chamber deployment and sampling
  • Laboratory protocols for GHG analysis, TA titration, spectrophotometric pH, nutrients, PIC/POC/DIC
  • Data processing workflows (R scripts, carbonate system calculations, statistical analyses)
How recorded:
  • Protocols will be uploaded to Protocols.io (AQUASERV community) when possible.
  • If Kristineberg protocols have DOIs/URLs, these will be cited.
  • If not publicly available, PDF copies will be included in the dataset.
  • All R scripts will include embedded metadata (package versions, settings).
6. Integration into repository metadata
When depositing datasets, I will include:
  • WHO, WHEN, WHERE metadata
  • Full methodological descriptions
  • Instrument metadata
  • Sample IDs and parameter lists
  • Links to protocols
  • Links to code 
  • Cross‑references between datasets and derived products
I will publish my methods in protocols.io and my analyses scripts and software will be stored on GitHub and published via institutional repositories.

The datasets described in Section 1.1.1 will be created through a combination of in situ field measurements, laboratory analyses, and computational processing carried out during the 3‑month research stay at Kristineberg Marine Research Station.

1. Field Data Creation
Benthic chamber incubations (in situ)
Data will be generated through controlled 24‑hour incubations using benthic chambers deployed in seagrass meadows and non‑vegetated sediments.
These chambers will produce:
  • Time‑series measurements of DIC, TA, pH
  • Greenhouse gas concentrations (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O)
  • Nutrients (PO₄, NH₄, NO₃, NO₂, SiO₂)
  • Chlorophyll, PIC, POC, DIC in sediments and water
  • Water samples will be collected at eight time points to capture diel cycles.
Multiparameter sensor deployments
Sensors placed next to the chambers will continuously record (These instruments generate high‑frequency environmental time series):
  • Temperature
  • Salinity
  • Dissolved oxygen
  • Irradiance
  • pH
2. Laboratory Data Creation
All laboratory analyses will be performed at Kristineberg’s accredited facilities.
  • Greenhouse gas analysis: CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O concentrations will be measured using a Picarro GHG analyser. Outputs include raw concentration files and processed flux data.
  • Carbonate chemistry: Spectrophotometric pH measurements, total alkalinity via automatic titrators, PIC, POC, DIC analyses on filtered water and sediment samples, chlorophyll quantification.
  • Nutrient analysis: PO₄, NH₄, NO₃, NO₂, SiO₂ will be analysed at SWEDAC‑accredited laboratories, producing certified concentration datasets.
These laboratory outputs form the core of the biogeochemical dataset.

3. Derived and Processed Data Creation
  • Flux calculations. Fluxes of DIC, TA, GHGs, nutrients, and carbon pools will be calculated from chamber time‑series data using: linear regressions, chamber volume and surface area, temperature‑corrected solubility constants.
  • Carbonate system modelling. Using the seacarb package in R, the project will compute: pCO₂, Ωaragonite / Ωcalcite, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, CO₂(aq), Revelle factor, Buffer capacity
  • Statistical analyses. Factorial analyses comparing treatments (vegetated vs non‑vegetated; present vs future conditions), descriptive statistics and variability summaries, visualisations (time series, flux plots, carbonate system diagrams)
These processed datasets will be stored in CSV, XLSX, and RDS formats.

The project will generate a wide range of environmental, biogeochemical, and analytical data derived from field incubations, laboratory analyses, and subsequent data processing. No external datasets will be reused beyond standard environmental baselines or climate projections already publicly available.

1. Field Data (raw and processed)
Collected during benthic chamber incubations and multiparameter sensor deployments in seagrass meadows.
Benthic chamber time‑series measurements of:
  • DIC, TA, pH
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O)
  • Nutrients (PO₄, NH₄, NO₃, NO₂, SiO₂)
  • PIC, POC, DIC in sediments and water
  • Chlorophyll
Format: CSV, XLSX, instrument‑generated text files (e.g., .txt, .dat)

Multiparameter sensor data (temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, irradiance, pH)
Format: CSV, TXT, proprietary sensor exports

Field metadata (GPS coordinates, deployment logs, environmental notes)
Format: CSV, TXT, PDF

2. Laboratory Analytical Data
Generated at Kristineberg’s accredited facilities.
  • Picarro GHG analyser outputs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O), Format: CSV, TXT, proprietary instrument files
  • Spectrophotometric pH and total alkalinity titration data, Format: CSV, XLSX
  • Nutrient concentrations from SWEDAC‑accredited labs, Format: PDF reports, CSV, XLSX
  • Carbonate chemistry measurements (PIC, POC, DIC), Format: CSV, XLSX
3. Derived and Processed Data
Generated during data analysis
  • Flux calculations (DIC, TA, GHGs, nutrients, carbon pools), Format: CSV, XLSX, RDS
  • Carbonate system parameters computed using seacarb, Format: CSV, RDS
  • Statistical outputs (regressions, factorial analyses, descriptive statistics), Format: CSV tables, R scripts (.R), R Markdown (.Rmd)
  • Figures and visualisations, Format: PNG, PDF
4. Documentation and Metadata
  • Sampling protocols, chamber deployment logs, laboratory protocols
  • Data dictionaries, README files, variable definitions, units
  • Workflow documentation and codebooks
Format: PDF, TXT, DOCX, Markdown (.md)

The project is expected to generate a moderate amount of data, typical for environmental biogeochemistry studies combining field incubations, high‑frequency sensors, and laboratory analyses. Based on the planned measurements, instrumentation, and processing steps, the total data volume is estimated at: ~10–25 GB
